arXiv:2604.01683v1 [cs.LG] 02 Apr 2026

Coupled Query-Key Dynamics for Attention

Barak Gahtan Affiliation: Technion – Israel Institute of Technology Email: barakgahtan@cs.technion.ac.il    Alex M. Bronstein Affiliation: Technion – Israel Institute of Technology Affiliation: ISTA – Institute of Science and Technology Austria Email: bron@cs.technion.ac.il
Abstract

Standard scaled dot-product attention computes scores from static, independent projections of the input. We show that evolving queries and keys jointly through shared learned dynamics before scoring - which we call coupled QK dynamics - improves language modeling perplexity and training stability. On WikiText-103 at 60M parameters, coupled dynamics achieves 22.55–22.62 perplexity vs. 24.22 for standard attention (−-6.6–6.9%), with only 0.11% additional parameters (shared across both instantiations). A structural ablation isolates coupling as the active ingredient: a symplectic (Hamiltonian) and a non-symplectic (Euler) integrator perform identically when both couple Q and K, while an uncoupled MLP baseline of matched capacity reaches only 23.81 with 8×\times higher seed variance. The integration step count (1–7) is similarly irrelevant - a single coupled step suffices. A compute-matched comparison reveals that coupling is a sample-efficiency mechanism: standard attention trained for 2.4×\times longer (matching wall-clock) reaches the same perplexity, but requires 2.4×\times more tokens. The advantage scales to 150M (−-6.7%) but narrows at 350M (−-1.0%), where Differential Attention (18.93) overtakes coupled dynamics (19.35). The benefit is corpus-dependent: coupling helps on domain-coherent text (WikiText-103 −-6.6%, PubMed −-4.5%) but degrades on heterogeneous web text (++10.3%) and shows no benefit on GLUE. We characterize when coupling helps and when it does not, providing practical guidelines.

1 Introduction

The attention mechanism (Vaswani et al., 2017) is the core computational primitive of modern transformers. Despite its empirical success, standard scaled dot-product attention exhibits well-documented structural pathologies. Attention weights converge toward uniform distributions as context grows, causing representational collapse (Dong et al., 2021). Spectral analysis reveals a widening gap between the leading singular values of the attention matrix - a failure mode unique to softmax that worsens with both depth and sequence length (Nait Saada et al., 2024). Pathologically low attention entropy destabilizes training, as the fixed 1/dk1/\sqrt{d_{k}} temperature provides no adaptive mechanism to prevent collapse (Zhai et al., 2023). These are not edge cases: attention sinks, hallucinations, and head redundancy are downstream symptoms of the same missing structural guarantees.

Recent work has addressed these issues along two axes: efficiency - reducing memory and compute via head sharing (Ainslie et al., 2023), KV compression (Liu and others, 2024), or optimized kernels (Dao et al., 2022) - and quality - improving the scoring function via noise cancellation (Ye et al., 2025) or learnable temperature (Sun and others, 2024). However, both lines treat modifications as engineering heuristics. Recent spectral analysis suggests that methods like Differential Attention implicitly address the spectral gap problem (Nait Saada et al., 2024), but without a principled framework, these improvements remain ad hoc.

A coupling lens for attention.

Standard attention computes queries and keys as independent linear projections of the input - they never interact before the dot product that produces attention scores. In physical systems, conjugate variables such as position and momentum co-evolve through shared dynamics, each influencing the other’s trajectory. This correspondence inspired us to try the same for Q and K: evolve them jointly through shared learned dynamics before scoring. The Hamiltonian formulation was our entry point, but ablations reveal that the benefit comes from coupling itself, not from the physics - a non-symplectic Euler integrator matches the symplectic Hamiltonian one exactly.

Contributions.

(1) Coupled QK Dynamics (§2.1): A framework that evolves Q and K jointly through shared learned dynamics before scoring. We instantiate it with two integrators - Hamiltonian (symplectic leapfrog) and Euler (non-symplectic) - and show both achieve comparable improvements over standard attention (22.55–22.62 vs. 24.22 at 60M scale, −-6.6–6.9%).

(2) Structural ablation isolating coupling (§3.1): We show that coupling is necessary (uncoupled MLP: +1.3 PPL, 8×\times higher variance), symplecticity is irrelevant (Euler matches Hamiltonian), and step count does not matter (n=1n{=}1 through n=7n{=}7 flat).

(3) Characterization of scope: Coupled dynamics helps on domain-coherent corpora (WikiText-103 −-6.6%, PubMed −-4.5%) but degrades on heterogeneous web text (OpenWebText ++10.3%) and shows no GLUE benefit. At 350M, Differential Attention overtakes. We distinguish pre-scoring enrichment (corpus-sensitive) from post-scoring noise cancellation (corpus-robust).

We evaluate on MQAR (Arora et al., 2024) associative recall, WikiText-103 (Merity et al., 2017) language modeling at 60M, 150M, and 350M parameters, OpenWebText (Gokaslan and Cohen, 2019), and GLUE downstream tasks. We compare against GQA (Ainslie et al., 2023) and Differential Attention (Ye et al., 2025), and include structural ablations (Euler, MLP-Only, step count) and RoPE compatibility tests.

2 Method

Preliminaries.

Standard scaled dot-product attention (Vaswani et al., 2017) computes

Attn⁡(Q,K,V)=softmax⁡(Q​K⊤dk)​V,\mathrm{Attn}(Q,K,V)=\mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{k}}}\right)V, (1)

where the fixed scaling 1/dk1/\sqrt{d_{k}} ensures unit-variance logits at initialization but provides no mechanism for adapting attention sharpness to layer depth or task demands. We propose coupled QK dynamics: evolving queries and keys jointly through shared learned dynamics before scoring. The key insight is that standard attention treats QQ and KK as independent static projections; coupling them through a shared transformation enriches the representational space available for scoring.

2.1 Coupled QK Dynamics

Motivation.

In standard attention, QQ and KK are independent linear projections of the input. Dong et al. (2021) show these projections suffer from rank collapse as depth increases. We propose enriching them by letting QQ and KK interact through a shared dynamical system before scoring.

The core structural property is indirect coupling: QQ’s update uses KK as a velocity, while KK’s update uses a learned coupling function f⁡(Q)f(Q). This creates an information exchange between query and key spaces - QQ moves according to KK, and KK is deflected by f⁡(Q)f(Q) - enriching both representations before scoring. This is in contrast to uncoupled approaches that transform QQ or KK independently.

General formulation.

Given QQ, KK from standard linear projections, we apply nn steps of a coupled update rule:

qt+1=qt+Δ​t⋅kt,kt+1=kt+Δ​t⋅f⁡(qt),q_{t+1}=q_{t}+\Delta t\cdot k_{t},\qquad k_{t+1}=k_{t}+\Delta t\cdot f(q_{t}), (2)

The step size Δ​t=exp⁡(τh)\Delta t=\exp(\tau_{h}) is a learnable per-head scalar. After nn steps, the evolved (qn,kn)(q_{n},k_{n}) replace the original QQ, KK in standard scaled dot-product scoring.

We instantiate this framework with two integrators that differ in their coupling structure: a Hamiltonian (leapfrog) integrator and a forward Euler integrator. As we show in §3.1, both achieve comparable performance.

2.2 Instantiations

Hamiltonian (leapfrog).

Inspired by Hamiltonian mechanics, we treat QQ as generalized position and KK as generalized momentum with a separable Hamiltonian H⁡(q,k)=12​‖k‖2+V⁡(q)H(q,k)=\tfrac{1}{2}\|k\|^{2}+V(q). A leapfrog (Störmer–Verlet) integrator evolves (Q,K)(Q,K) for nn steps:

kt+12=kt+Δ​t2​f​(qt),qt+1=qt+Δ​t⋅kt+12,kt+1=kt+12+Δ​t2​f​(qt+1),k_{t+\frac{1}{2}}=k_{t}+\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\,f(q_{t}),\qquad q_{t+1}=q_{t}+\Delta t\cdot k_{t+\frac{1}{2}},\qquad k_{t+1}=k_{t+\frac{1}{2}}+\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\,f(q_{t+1}), (3)

where f⁡(q)f(q) is a two-layer MLP with SiLU activation that models the coupling from queries to keys. This integrator is symplectic (volume-preserving), which historically motivated our investigation; however, our ablations show this property is not the source of the improvement (§3.1).

Euler (non-symplectic).

The simplest coupled integrator applies forward Euler updates:

qt+1=qt+Δ​t⋅kt,kt+1=kt+Δ​t⋅f⁡(qt).q_{t+1}=q_{t}+\Delta t\cdot k_{t},\qquad k_{t+1}=k_{t}+\Delta t\cdot f(q_{t}). (4)

This uses the same coupling network f⁡(q)f(q) and learnable step size as the Hamiltonian variant, but is not symplectic - it does not preserve phase-space volume. Euler matches Hamiltonian in perplexity (§3.1), confirming that symplecticity is unnecessary.

Coupling network.

Both instantiations share the same coupling network f⁡(q)f(q): a two-layer MLP (dk→dkd_{k}\to d_{k}) with SiLU activation and no bias, operating independently per head. This adds 0.11% parameters at 60M scale. The coupling network is a learned function that mediates the interaction between QQ and KK without requiring an explicit potential function or its gradient.

2.3 Ablation Baselines

To isolate the effect of coupling, we compare against:

MLP-Only applies the same two-layer MLP to queries as a residual update (q′=q+f⁡(q)q^{\prime}=q+f(q)) without modifying keys. This has identical parameter count to the coupled variants but no Q-K coupling, testing whether the improvement comes from added nonlinear capacity or from coupling.

Standard Attention uses QQ, KK directly from linear projections with no pre-scoring enrichment.

We also compare against two published baselines that modify attention through different mechanisms: Grouped Query Attention (GQA) (Ainslie et al., 2023), which shares KV projections across head groups, and Differential Attention (Ye et al., 2025), which cancels noise via dual-softmax post-scoring - a complementary axis to our pre-scoring coupled dynamics.

3 Experiments

3.1 Structural Ablation: Coupling Is the Active Ingredient

We conduct a controlled ablation at 60M scale on WikiText-103 to isolate what drives the improvement. Table 1 compares six configurations that vary along two axes: (1) whether Q and K are coupled through shared dynamics before scoring, and (2) whether that coupling is symplectic.

Three findings emerge:

(1) Coupled ≫\gg uncoupled. Both coupled methods (Euler 22.55, Hamiltonian 22.62) outperform all uncoupled methods (23.81–24.66) by a wide margin. The best uncoupled method, MLP-Only (23.81), still trails the worst coupled method by 1.19 PPL. This confirms that coupling Q and K through shared dynamics before scoring - not additional capacity or integration scheme - is the mechanism driving the improvement.

(2) Euler ≈\approx Hamiltonian. The non-symplectic Euler integrator matches the symplectic Hamiltonian within noise (22.55 vs. 22.62). Volume preservation provides no measurable benefit; the coupling structure alone drives the improvement.

(3) Coupling stabilizes training. Both coupled methods exhibit remarkably low variance (std 0.04) compared to MLP-Only (std 0.31, an 8×8\times increase). The shared dynamics constrain the joint QK trajectory, reducing sensitivity to initialization.

Step count ablation.

Table 2 varies the number of integration steps in the Hamiltonian variant. A single step suffices; additional steps provide no benefit.

Performance is flat across n=1n=1 to 77 (22.56–22.62), indicating that a single coupled update captures the essential interaction. This is consistent with the Euler result above: the coupling structure matters, not the fidelity of the integration. A single step also minimizes computational overhead.

MLP capacity analysis.

To obtain a robust estimate of the uncoupled baseline, we train MLP-Only across 10 seeds (mean 23.81, std 0.31). A two-sample tt-test against Hamiltonian (3 seeds, mean 22.62, std 0.04) yields p<0.001p<0.001, confirming that coupling provides a statistically significant improvement beyond what added MLP capacity alone explains.

3.2 Language Modeling

We evaluate on two corpora: WikiText-103 (Merity et al., 2017) (100M tokens, curated) and OpenWebText (Gokaslan and Cohen, 2019) (100M token subset, web-scale). Both use GPT-2 BPE tokenization (vocab=50,257) with cosine LR schedule. All variants share identical training infrastructure, differing only in the attention mechanism.

Figure 1 shows the 60M convergence dynamics (perplexity values are in Table 1).
